positions/pacifism/oneLine: Jesus’ command to love enemies and his refusal of the sword forbid his followers from killing, including in war; Christians overcome evil with good.
positions/pacifism/coreClaims/0: Jesus’ teaching and example of nonviolent love are normative for all disciples, not only for a spiritual elite or private life.
positions/pacifism/coreClaims/1: The cross shows God overcoming evil by suffering love rather than violence.
positions/pacifism/coreClaims/2: Christians may not kill in war or capital punishment; many also refuse coercive office (nonresistance) while others practise active nonviolent resistance.
positions/pacifism/coreClaims/3: The Church is called to be a peaceable community that witnesses to the coming kingdom.
positions/pacifism/origin: Pre-Constantinian writers (Justin, Tertullian, Origen, Lactantius) and the Apostolic Tradition (c.215) opposed Christians killing. After Constantine, nonviolence was largely confined to clergy and monks, then revived by the Waldensians, the Czech Brethren (Petr Chelčický), the Anabaptists (Schleitheim, 1527), Quakers (1661) and Church of the Brethren (1708). In the 20th century it was renewed by Tolstoy, Dorothy Day’s Catholic Worker, Martin Luther King Jr. and John Howard Yoder’s Politics of Jesus (1972).
positions/pacifism/proponentsOther/4: Leo Tolstoy (excommunicated by the Russian Synod, 1901)
positions/pacifism/strongestArguments/0: It takes the plainest words of Jesus at face value and follows the pattern of the cross.
positions/pacifism/strongestArguments/1: It was the dominant view of the Church’s leading writers for its first three centuries.
positions/pacifism/strongestArguments/2: Nonviolent movements (abolitionists, King, the fall of Communism in 1989, the Philippines 1986) have achieved real change.
positions/pacifism/strongestArguments/3: It avoids the historic complicity of churches in crusades, conquest and nationalism.
positions/pacifism/strongestObjections/0: Just-war thinkers argue that it abandons the innocent to aggressors, as critics of pacifism in the face of Nazism (Niebuhr) insisted.
positions/pacifism/strongestObjections/1: The New Testament does not tell soldiers to leave the army (Luke 3:14; Acts 10) and affirms the ruler’s sword (Rom 13:4).
positions/pacifism/strongestObjections/2: Pacifist communities often benefit from protection provided by others’ use of force.
positions/pacifism/strongestObjections/3: Early-church evidence is mixed: Christians served in the army by the late 2nd century, and objections partly concerned idolatry rather than killing.
positions/pacifism/responses/0: Pacifists reply that the Christian vocation is faithfulness, not control of history, and that nonviolent action is far from passive (e.g. Le Chambon-sur-Lignon sheltered thousands of Jews, 1940–44).
positions/pacifism/responses/1: They argue Romans 13 describes God’s providential use of rulers without commanding Christians to wield the sword, and that Romans 12:19–21 immediately precedes it.
positions/pacifism/consequences/0: Generated the historic peace churches and conscientious objection, recognised in law in many countries (Mennonite Central Committee; alternative civilian service).
positions/pacifism/consequences/1: Inspired major nonviolent movements, including US civil rights.
positions/pacifism/consequences/2: Shapes contemporary Catholic and Protestant peace-building and critiques of nuclear weapons.
positions/constantinian-synthesis/oneLin: Church and Christian state are partners in one Christian society: rulers protect and promote the true faith, and the Church sanctifies and guides rulers.
positions/constantinian-synthesis/coreCl: God raised up Christian rulers to protect the Church and promote true religion.
Church and state are two distinct but harmonious authorities in a single Christian commonwealth (Byzantine "symphony"; Western "two swords").
Rulers may convene councils, enforce orthodoxy and punish heresy and public sin.
Society’s law, calendar and culture should be shaped by Christian faith.
positions/constantinian-synthesis/keyTex: Isaiah 49:23 ("kings shall be thy nursing fathers")
Eusebius, Oration in Praise of Constantine (336)
positions/constantinian-synthesis/origin: After Constantine’s conversion (312) and the Edict of Milan (313), Eusebius of Caesarea articulated a Christian imperial theology in which the emperor mirrored the Logos. Theodosius I made Nicene Christianity the state religion (380); Justinian’s Novel 6 (535) described the "symphony" of priesthood and empire. The pattern continued in Byzantium, Russia ("Third Rome"), Ethiopia (the Solomonic monarchy), the Carolingian and medieval West, and in Reformation established churches.
positions/constantinian-synthesis/propon: Pope Boniface VIII (papal form, Unam Sanctam 1302)
positions/constantinian-synthesis/strong: It ended persecution and allowed Christianity to shape law (e.g. abolishing crucifixion and gladiatorial games, Sunday rest, care for the poor through church institutions).
If Christ is Lord of all, a society’s public life should acknowledge him, not only private hearts.
It produced the civilisations of Byzantium, Ethiopia, Armenia and medieval Europe, including universities, hospitals and law.

Anabaptists, Kierkegaard (Attack upon "Christendom", 1854–55) and Yoder argue that it betrayed the Church’s calling, turning a persecuted minority into a persecuting establishment and diluting discipleship.
It legitimised coercion of heretics, Jews and pagans, crusades and wars of religion.
Rulers routinely manipulated the Church for political ends (Byzantine caesaropapism, Henry VIII).
positions/constantinian-synthesis/respon: Defenders reply that the alternative is not neutrality but some other public creed, and that Christian establishment has often coexisted with religious liberty (e.g. modern England, Scandinavia).

They argue that the abuses were failures to live up to Christian principles, which themselves supplied the resources for later reform (e.g. Ambrose disciplining Theodosius after the Thessalonica massacre, 390).
positions/constantinian-synthesis/conseq: Shaped all major Christian civilisations for over a millennium.
Produced conflicts between popes and emperors (Investiture Controversy) and between church and state in Byzantium.
Its decline (French Revolution, disestablishment, secularisation) is a central theme of modern church history.
Remains an ideal or a warning in debates on Christian nationalism.
positions/two-kingdoms/oneLine: God governs the world in two ways: through the spiritual government of the gospel, which creates faith, and the temporal government of law and the sword, which preserves order. Christians live in both and must not confuse them.
positions/two-kingdoms/coreClaims/0: God’s "right hand" rule is the gospel, Word and sacraments, forming the Church by faith without coercion.
positions/two-kingdoms/coreClaims/1: God’s "left hand" rule is temporal government: law, reason and the sword restraining evil for the common good.
positions/two-kingdoms/coreClaims/2: The Church must not wield the sword, and the state must not rule consciences or dictate doctrine.
positions/two-kingdoms/coreClaims/3: Christians may serve as rulers, judges and soldiers as a vocation of love for neighbour.
positions/two-kingdoms/coreClaims/4: Obedience to rulers is required except where they command sin (Acts 5:29).
positions/two-kingdoms/origin: Building on Augustine’s two cities and Gelasius’ two powers, Martin Luther set out the doctrine in Temporal Authority (1523) and applied it to the Peasants’ War (1525). Lutheran confessions (Augsburg XVI, XXVIII) embody it; Calvin’s "twofold government" (Institutes 3.19.15; 4.20) is a Reformed counterpart. In recent decades David VanDrunen and others have revived a Reformed "two kingdoms" approach.
positions/two-kingdoms/proponentsOther/0: Eivind Berggrav (used it to resist Nazi occupation in Norway, 1942)
positions/two-kingdoms/strongestArgument: It protects the gospel from politicisation and the state from clerical domination.
It grounds Christian service in ordinary vocations, honouring secular work and government as God’s good gifts.
It reflects Jesus’ distinction between Caesar and God and his kingdom "not of this world".
positions/two-kingdoms/strongestObjectio: Critics (including Karl Barth and many historians) argue it fostered political quietism and deference to rulers, contributing to German Lutheran passivity under Nazism.
Luther’s own harsh tract Against the Murderous, Thieving Hordes of Peasants (1525) is cited as an example of siding with power.
Reformed transformationists (Kuyper) and liberationists argue that Christ’s lordship extends to political life and must shape it, not only the gospel.
positions/two-kingdoms/responses/0: Lutherans reply that the doctrine also limits the state, as Norwegian bishops and Bonhoeffer used it to resist tyranny.
positions/two-kingdoms/responses/1: They argue that failures under Nazism owed more to nationalism, the "orders of creation" theology of some theologians and fear than to Luther’s distinction itself.
positions/two-kingdoms/consequences/0: Shaped Lutheran state churches and the Protestant ethic of vocation.
positions/two-kingdoms/consequences/1: Influenced the modern distinction between church and state.
positions/two-kingdoms/consequences/2: Remains a reference point in debates on Christian political engagement.
positions/anabaptist-separation/oneLine: The Church is a voluntary community of disciples separated from the world: it renounces the sword, oaths and magistracy, and witnesses to Christ’s kingdom by its life together.
positions/anabaptist-separation/coreClai: There are two orders: the perfection of Christ (the Church) and the world, where God ordains the sword outside Christ’s perfection.
Disciples do not use lethal force, swear oaths or hold coercive office (Schleitheim 6–7).
The Church is gathered by voluntary believer’s baptism and kept pure by loving discipline (the ban).
Faithfulness, not effectiveness or control of society, is the Christian’s calling; suffering is expected.
positions/anabaptist-separation/origin: Swiss Brethren in Zurich (first adult baptisms, January 1525) under Conrad Grebel, Felix Manz and George Blaurock broke with Zwingli; Michael Sattler’s Schleitheim Confession (1527) set out their separatist ethic. After Münster (1535), Menno Simons consolidated nonresistant Anabaptism in the Netherlands. Hutterites (from 1528) adopted community of goods; the Amish split from Swiss Mennonites under Jacob Ammann (1693).
positions/anabaptist-separation/stronges: It embodies the Sermon on the Mount as a communal way of life rather than an impossible ideal.
It resisted the coercive Christendom that persecuted dissenters and refused to kill even its persecutors.
Its witness for religious liberty and voluntary church membership has been vindicated by modern democracies.
Magisterial Reformers (Augsburg XVI; Belgic Confession 36) argued it rejected God’s ordinance of government and abandoned neighbours to injustice.
Critics call it sectarian, withdrawing from responsibility for the common good while relying on state protection.
Its strict discipline (shunning) has been criticised as harsh and divisive.
positions/anabaptist-separation/response: Anabaptists reply that they serve the common good through mutual aid, relief and service (e.g. Mennonite Central Committee, 1920) and that their witness to peace is itself a public good.
Modern Anabaptist theologians (Yoder) argue the Church is a "social ethic" in itself, a political alternative rather than a withdrawal.
positions/anabaptist-separation/conseque: Thousands of Anabaptists were executed by Catholic and Protestant authorities in the 16th century; the Martyrs Mirror (1660) preserved their memory.
Produced the Mennonite, Amish and Hutterite communities, now present across the Americas, Africa (e.g. Ethiopia’s Meserete Kristos Church) and Asia.
Influenced Baptist and free-church ideas of religious liberty and separation of church and state.
